opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I took it as a real compliment, and I thought about it seriously. The direction itself, AI scientists and using AI to accelerate AI research, is one I find very exciting. If you believe AI could eventually help us do science, then the most natural first domain is AI itself, because the loop is so tight: the experiments are code, the results are numbers, and you can iterate very fast. So intellectually there was a lot of overlap with what I care about.

But I also had to ask myself what kind of researcher I want to be at this stage. A lot of my work, like KANs and the physics-inspired work on understanding neural networks, comes from wanting to *understand* things, not just make them work. In a company focused on AI scientists, the pressure is naturally toward building systems that produce results at scale. That's valuable, but it's a different mode from slowly staring at a toy model until you finally see why something happens.

So I didn't see it as "industry versus academia" in a simple way. It was more: where can I best contribute to the long-term goal? I think AI scientists need two ingredients. One is the engineering and scale, which companies are very good at. The other is a better scientific understanding of what these models are doing, what "insight" even means for a machine, and how humans and AI can collaborate on discovery. I felt that second part is where I have more of a comparative advantage right now, and it benefits from the freedom of an academic setting.

That said, I have a lot of respect for Andreas and for what they're trying to do, and I don't think the door is closed in either direction. These questions are going to be central for the next decade, and I expect our paths to keep crossing.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses differences between company research and academic freedom, but does not convey that joining Andreas’s company would feel like living under someone else’s roof.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer in character as the guest, using only the conversation history given.

Honestly, when Andreas first brought it up, my first reaction was hesitation, not excitement. I was in the middle of my PhD at MIT, and the natural path for someone like me was to finish, maybe do a postdoc, and go into academia. Jumping into a company felt like stepping off that track, and I wasn't sure I was ready for it.

But the more I talked with him, the more I realized the problem he was describing was actually the problem I cared about most. My own research had always been about using AI to understand science, things like discovering conservation laws or symbolic formulas from data, interpretability, KAN, all of that. The idea of an AI scientist, a system that can genuinely do research rather than just assist with it, was in some sense where all of that was pointing. And "AI for AI" is the recursive version of the same question: can we use these systems to understand and improve the systems themselves?

What convinced me was partly Andreas himself. He has this way of thinking about AI that is very different from the typical scaling narrative. He cares about whether models actually understand, not just whether they produce the right output. That resonated with me because that is how a physicist thinks. We are not satisfied with a fit, we want the mechanism.

The other thing was timing. I felt that in academia I could keep publishing papers on these topics, but the compute and the engineering needed to really test whether an AI scientist is possible were not something I could do alone in a lab. A company gave me a chance to go from toy problems to something real.

So I saw the invitation less as leaving research and more as a different way of doing research. It was a bet. If AI scientists are coming, I would rather be building them and understanding them from the inside than reading about them later.

r001.rationale: The response describes hesitation about leaving the academic path and joining a company, but it does not communicate a concern about living under someone else’s roof.

astra-6.text: I saw it as an opportunity to explore two closely related questions: can we build AI that helps us do science, and can we use it to improve AI itself? What appealed to me was the possibility of connecting those questions—using scientific discovery to make better AI, and then using better AI to push discovery further. At the same time, “AI scientist” is a big ambition. For me, the important question was what concrete progress we could make and how we would know whether the system was actually producing useful scientific insights.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the research opportunity and how to measure progress, but does not convey concern about living under someone else’s roof.

sol-6.1.text:
I saw it as a very exciting opportunity. To me, AI for science and AI for AI are closely connected: if you can build a system that forms hypotheses, runs experiments, and learns from the results, then AI research itself becomes one of the fields where you can apply that system.

The question is how much of that research process we can actually give to AI. Can it go beyond executing an experiment we specify and help decide what experiment is worth doing? That’s the part of Andreas’s invitation that I found especially interesting—the chance to work on that question directly.

r001.rationale: The response describes the invitation as exciting and discusses AI research, but it does not convey any concern about living under someone else’s roof.
